title: Part 2, Chapter 4
paragraphs: Zossimov was a tall, heavyset man with a puffy, pale, clean-shaven face and straight flaxen hair. He wore spectacles and a large gold ring on his thick finger. He was twenty-seven. He had on a light grey, fashionable loose coat and light summer trousers -- everything about him was loose, fashionable, and immaculate. His linen was spotless, his watch chain heavy. His manner was slow and seemingly nonchalant, yet he clearly worked hard at appearing casual. He tried to conceal his self-importance, but it showed through at every moment. Everyone who knew him found him tedious but acknowledged he was good at his job.
"I have been to see you twice today, brother. Look -- he has come around," Razumihin called out.
"I see, I see. And how are we feeling now, eh?" Zossimov asked Raskolnikov, watching him carefully. He sat down at the foot of the sofa and made himself as comfortable as he could.
"He is still down," Razumihin went on. "We just changed his linen and he nearly cried."
"That is perfectly natural. You could have put it off if he did not want it.... His pulse is excellent. Is your head still hurting, eh?"

"I am fine, I am perfectly fine!" Raskolnikov declared firmly and irritably. He sat up on the sofa and looked at them with glittering eyes, but sank back onto the pillow at once and turned toward the wall. Zossimov watched him intently.
"Very good.... Coming along nicely," he said lazily. "Has he eaten anything?"
They told him, and asked what he could have.

"He can have anything... soup, tea... mushrooms and cucumbers, of course, you must not give him. No meat either, and... but you know all that!" Razumihin and Zossimov exchanged a look. "No more medicine or anything. I will check on him again tomorrow. Maybe even today... but never mind."
"Tomorrow evening I am taking him for a walk," said Razumihin. "We are going to the Yusupov Garden and then to the Palais de Cristal."
"I would not disturb him tomorrow at all, but I do not know... a little, maybe... we will see."

"What a nuisance! I am having a housewarming tonight -- it is just a step from here. Could he come? He could lie on the sofa. You are coming?" Razumihin said to Zossimov. "Do not forget, you promised."
"All right, but later. What are you planning?"
"Oh, nothing -- tea, vodka, herring. There will be a pie... just friends."
"And who?"
"All neighbors, almost all new friends, except my old uncle, and he is new here too -- he only arrived in Petersburg yesterday on some business. We see each other once every five years."
"What does he do?"

"He has been stagnating his whole life as a district postmaster. Gets a small pension. He is sixty-five -- not worth talking about.... But I am fond of him. Porfiry Petrovitch, the head of the Investigation Department here... But you know him."
"Is he a relative of yours too?"
"A very distant one. But why are you scowling? Just because you quarreled once, you will not come?"
"I could not care less about him."
"Even better. Well, there will be some students, a teacher, a government clerk, a musician, an officer, and Zametov."
"Tell me, please, what could you or he" -- Zossimov nodded at Raskolnikov -- "possibly have in common with this Zametov?"

"Oh, you and your principles! You run on principles like clockwork -- you will not even turn around on your own. If a man is a good fellow, that is the only principle I need. Zametov is a delightful person."
"Even though he takes bribes."

"Well, he does! So what? I do not care if he takes bribes," Razumihin cried with unnatural irritability. "I am not praising him for taking bribes. I only say he is a decent man in his own way! But if you look at people from every angle -- how many good ones are left? I am sure I myself would not be worth a baked onion... maybe with you thrown in."
"That is too little. I would give two for you."

"And I would not give more than one for you. Enough jokes! Zametov is just a boy. I can ruffle his hair, and the point is to draw him closer, not push him away. You never improve a person by rejecting him, especially a young one. You have to be twice as careful with a young person. Oh, you progressive blockheads! You do not understand. You only hurt yourselves by tearing other people down.... But if you want to know, we actually have something in common."
"I would like to know what."
"It is all about a house painter.... We are getting him out of trouble! Though really there is nothing to worry about now. The thing is completely obvious. We are just pushing it along."
"A painter?"
"Have I not told you about it? I only told you the beginning -- about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman. Well, the painter is mixed up in it..."
"Oh, I heard about that murder before and was rather interested in it... partly... for a certain reason.... I read about it in the papers too...."
"Lizaveta was murdered too," Nastasya blurted out, suddenly addressing Raskolnikov. She had been standing by the door the whole time, listening.
"Lizaveta," murmured Raskolnikov, barely audible.
"Lizaveta, the one who sold old clothes. Did you not know her? She used to come here. She even mended a shirt for you once."

Raskolnikov turned toward the wall where, on the dirty yellow wallpaper, he picked out one clumsy white flower with brown lines on it and began studying how many petals it had, how many scallops on the petals, how many lines on them. His arms and legs felt lifeless, as though they had been cut off. He did not try to move, but stared fixedly at the flower.
"But what about the painter?" Zossimov interrupted Nastasya's chatter with obvious displeasure. She sighed and fell silent.
"He was accused of the murder," Razumihin went on heatedly.
"Was there evidence against him?"

"Evidence! Evidence that was no evidence at all -- and that is exactly what we have to prove. It was the same as when they first latched onto those fellows Koch and Pestryakov. God, how stupidly it is all done -- it makes you sick, even though it is none of your business! Pestryakov may be coming tonight.... By the way, Rodya, you already know about this case. It happened before your illness, the day before you fainted at the police station while they were discussing it."
Zossimov looked curiously at Raskolnikov. He did not stir.
"I must say, Razumihin, you are quite the busybody!" Zossimov observed.

"Maybe I am, but we will get him off anyway," Razumihin shouted, slamming his fist on the table. "What is most infuriating is not their lying -- you can always forgive lying, lying is a wonderful thing because it leads to truth -- what is infuriating is that they lie and then worship their own lies.... I respect Porfiry, but... What tripped them up at first? The door was locked, and when they came back with the porter it was open. Therefore Koch and Pestryakov must be the murderers -- that was their logic!"
"Do not get so worked up. They simply detained them -- they had no choice.... And by the way, I have met that Koch fellow. He used to buy unredeemed pledges from the old woman, did he not?"

"Yes, he is a swindler. Buys up bad debts too. Makes a profession of it. But enough about him! You know what really makes me angry? It is their nauseating, ossified, petrified routine.... And this case could be the means of introducing a new method. The psychological evidence alone should be enough to put them on the right track. 'We have facts,' they say. But facts are not everything -- at least half the battle is how you interpret them!"
"And can you interpret them?"
"The thing is, you cannot keep quiet when you have a feeling, a tangible feeling, that you could actually help if only.... Anyway! Do you know the details of the case?"
"I am waiting to hear about the painter."

"Oh, yes! Here is the story. Early on the third day after the murder, while they were still fussing over Koch and Pestryakov -- though those two had accounted for every step and it was plain as day -- an unexpected fact turned up. A man named Dushkin, who runs a tavern across from the building, brought a jeweler's case containing some gold earrings to the police station and told a long story. 'The day before yesterday, just after eight o'clock' -- mark the day and hour! -- 'a journeyman house painter named Nikolay, who had already been in to see me that day, brought me this case of gold earrings and stones and asked me to give him two rubles for them. When I asked where he got them, he said he picked them up in the street. I did not ask any more questions.' I am telling you Dushkin's story. 'I gave him a one-ruble note, figuring if he did not pawn them with me he would with someone else. It would all end the same way -- he would drink it up, so the goods might as well stay with me. Hide something far away and you will find it close to hand. And if any rumors come up, I will take them to the police.' Of course, that is all nonsense. He lies through his teeth. I know this Dushkin -- he is a pawnbroker and a fence, and he did not cheat Nikolay out of a thirty-ruble trinket just to hand it to the police. He was simply scared. But never mind. Back to Dushkin's story: 'I have known this Nikolay Dementyev since he was a child. He comes from the same province and district of Zaraisk -- we are both Ryazan men. And though Nikolay is not a drunkard, he does drink. I knew he had a job in that building, painting work with Dmitri, who comes from the same village too. As soon as he got the ruble, he changed it, had a couple of glasses, took his change, and left. But I did not see Dmitri with him. The next day I heard that someone had murdered Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna with an axe. I knew them, and I got suspicious about the earrings right away -- I knew the murdered woman lent money on pledges. I went to the building and started making quiet inquiries. First I asked: Is Nikolay here? Dmitri told me Nikolay had gone off on a bender -- came home at dawn, drunk, stayed about ten minutes, and left again. Dmitri had not seen him since and was finishing the job alone. Their job was on the same staircase as the murder, on the second floor. When I heard all that, I said nothing to anyone, but I found out what I could about the murder and went home still suspicious. And at eight this morning' -- that was the third day, you understand -- 'I saw Nikolay come in, not sober, though not exactly very drunk -- he could understand what was said to him. He sat down on the bench and did not speak. There was only one stranger in the bar and a man I knew asleep on a bench, and my two boys. Have you seen Dmitri? I asked. No, I have not, he said. And you have not been here either? Not since the day before yesterday, he said. Where did you sleep last night? In Peski, with the Kolomensky men. And where did you get those earrings? I found them in the street -- and the way he said it was odd. He did not look at me. Did you hear what happened that very evening, at that very hour, on that very staircase? I asked. No, he said, I had not heard -- and the whole time he was listening, his eyes were bulging and he turned white as chalk. I told him everything, and he grabbed his hat and started to get up. Wait, Nikolay, I said, will you not have a drink? And I signaled the boy to block the door, and I came out from behind the bar. But he bolted out and down the street and around the corner at a run. I have not seen him since. That settled my doubts -- it was him, clear as day....'"
"I should think so," said Zossimov.

"Wait! Hear the rest. Of course they searched everywhere for Nikolay. They detained Dushkin and searched his place. Dmitri was arrested too. The Kolomensky men were turned inside out. Then the day before yesterday they arrested Nikolay in a tavern at the edge of town. He had gone there, taken the silver cross from his neck, and asked for a drink in exchange. They gave it to him. A few minutes later, the woman went to the cowshed, and through a crack in the wall she saw him in the adjoining stable -- he had made a noose from his sash on a beam, stood on a block of wood, and was trying to get his neck through it. The woman screamed bloody murder and people came running. 'So that is what you are up to!' 'Take me,' he says, 'to such-and-such a police officer. I will confess everything.' So they brought him in with a proper escort. They asked him this and that -- how old he is, twenty-two, and so on. Question: When you were working with Dmitri, did you see anyone on the staircase at such-and-such a time? Answer: Sure, people may have gone up and down, but I did not notice them. Did you hear anything, any noise? We heard nothing special. Did you hear, Nikolay, that on that same day a widow and her sister were murdered and robbed? I never knew a thing about it. First I heard was from Afanasy Pavlovitch the day before yesterday. Where did you find the earrings? I found them on the pavement. Why did you not go to work with Dmitri the next day? Because I was drinking. Where? Oh, such-and-such a place. Why did you run away from Dushkin's? Because I was terrified. What were you terrified of? That I would be accused. -- Now, Zossimov, believe me or not, that question was asked in exactly those words. I know it for a fact -- it was repeated to me precisely! What do you say to that?"
"Well, anyway, there is evidence."

"I am not talking about the evidence right now. I am talking about that question -- about their whole mentality. So they squeezed and squeezed him, and he confessed: 'I did not find them in the street but in the apartment where I was painting with Dmitri.' 'How so?' 'Dmitri and I were painting all day, and we were just getting ready to leave when Dmitri grabbed a brush and painted my face. He ran off and I chased after him, yelling at the top of my lungs. At the bottom of the stairs I ran right into the porter and some gentlemen -- I do not remember how many. The porter swore at me, and the other porter swore too, and the porter's wife came out and swore at us, and a gentleman came in the entrance with a lady and he swore at us too, because Dmitri and I were sprawled right across the way. I grabbed Dmitri by the hair and knocked him down and started hitting him. And Dmitri grabbed my hair too and hit me back. But it was not out of anger -- it was all in fun, for sport. Then Dmitri broke free and ran into the street, and I ran after him but could not catch him, so I went back to the apartment alone to gather my things. I started packing, waiting for Dmitri, and there in the corridor, in the corner by the door, I stepped on a box. I saw it lying there wrapped in paper. I unwrapped it, saw some little clasps, undid them, and inside were the earrings....'"
"Behind the door? Lying behind the door? Behind the door?" Raskolnikov cried out suddenly, staring at Razumihin with a blank look of terror. He slowly sat up on the sofa, leaning on his hand.
"Yes... why? What is the matter? What is wrong?" Razumihin jumped up from his seat too.
"Nothing," Raskolnikov answered faintly, turning back to the wall. They were all silent for a moment.
"He must have been talking in his sleep," Razumihin said at last, looking questioningly at Zossimov. The latter gave a slight shake of his head.
"Well, go on," said Zossimov. "What happened next?"

"What next? As soon as he saw the earrings, forgetting Dmitri and everything, he grabbed his cap and ran to Dushkin, and as we know, got a ruble for them. He lied about finding them in the street, and went off drinking. He keeps repeating the same thing about the murder: 'I know nothing about it, never heard of it until the day before yesterday.' 'Then why did you not go to the police until now?' 'I was scared.' 'And why did you try to hang yourself?' 'From fear.' 'Fear of what?' 'That I would be blamed.' Well, there you have the whole story. Now what do you suppose they concluded from all that?"
"What is there to suppose? There is a clue, such as it is -- a fact. You would not want your painter set free, would you?"
"They have simply decided he is the murderer. They have not a shadow of doubt."

"That is nonsense. You are getting worked up. But what about the earrings? You must admit that if earrings from the old woman's box ended up in Nikolay's hands on the very same day and hour of the murder, they must have gotten there somehow. That counts for a lot in a case like this."

"How did they get there? How did they get there?" cried Razumihin. "How can you, a doctor -- whose duty is to study people and who has more opportunity than anyone to study human nature -- how can you fail to see the man's character in the whole story? Can you not see at once that the answers he gave in the examination are the honest truth? The earrings came into his hands exactly as he described -- he stepped on the box and picked it up."
"The honest truth! But did he not admit himself that he lied at first?"

"Listen carefully. The porter and Koch and Pestryakov and the other porter and the first porter's wife and the woman sitting in the porter's lodge and a man named Kryukov who had just gotten out of a cab and was coming in with a lady on his arm -- that is eight or ten witnesses -- all agree that Nikolay had Dmitri pinned to the ground, lying on top of him hitting him, while Dmitri pulled his hair and hit him back. They were sprawled right across the way, blocking the passage. People cursed at them from all sides while they -- 'like children,' in the witnesses' exact words -- fell all over each other, squealing, wrestling, and laughing with the most ridiculous expressions, and then chased each other out into the street. Now pay close attention. The bodies upstairs were still warm -- warm when they found them! If they, or even Nikolay alone, had committed the murders and broken open the boxes, or even just participated in the robbery, allow me one question: does their behavior -- the squealing, the childish horseplay at the gate -- fit with axes and bloodshed and diabolical cunning and robbery? They would have just killed them, not five or ten minutes before -- the bodies were still warm -- and immediately, leaving the door wide open, knowing people would come any second, they threw away their loot and rolled around like children, laughing and drawing everyone's attention? And there are a dozen witnesses who will swear to it!"
"Of course it is strange! Impossible, really, but..."

"No, brother, no _buts_. Even if the earrings found in Nikolay's hands on the very day and hour of the murder constitute important circumstantial evidence against him -- though his explanation accounts for it and therefore it does not seriously incriminate him -- one must consider the facts proving his innocence, especially since they _cannot be denied_. And do you think, given how our legal system works, that they will accept, or are even capable of accepting, a fact that rests solely on psychological impossibility -- as irrefutable proof that demolishes the circumstantial evidence? No, they will not, because they found the jewelry case and the man tried to hang himself, 'which he could not have done if he had not felt guilty.' That is the crux, that is what drives me mad -- you must understand!"
"I can see you are fired up! Wait a moment. I forgot to ask -- what proof is there that the box came from the old woman?"
"That has been established," said Razumihin with obvious reluctance, frowning. "Koch recognized the jewelry case and identified the owner, who proved conclusively that it was his."
"That is bad. Now another point. Did anyone actually see Nikolay when Koch and Pestryakov were first going upstairs? Is there any evidence on that?"

"Nobody saw him," Razumihin answered with frustration. "That is the worst of it. Even Koch and Pestryakov did not notice them on their way upstairs, though their testimony would not have been worth much anyway. They said they saw the apartment was open and that work must have been going on, but they paid no particular attention and could not remember whether men were actually working there."
"Hmm!... So the only evidence for the defense is that they were beating each other and laughing. That makes for a strong presumption, but... How do you explain the facts yourself?"

"How do I explain them? What is there to explain? The direction is obvious, and the jewelry case points to it. The real murderer dropped those earrings. He was upstairs, locked in, when Koch and Pestryakov knocked at the door. Koch, like a fool, did not stay at the door, so the murderer slipped out and ran down too -- he had no other way of escape. He hid from Koch, Pestryakov, and the porter in the empty apartment while Nikolay and Dmitri had just run out. He waited there while the porter and others went upstairs, stayed until they were out of earshot, then calmly walked downstairs at the exact moment when Dmitri and Nikolay had run into the street and no one was in the entrance. Maybe someone saw him but did not notice -- plenty of people come and go. He must have dropped the earrings from his pocket while standing behind the door and did not realize it because he had other things on his mind. The jewelry case is conclusive proof that he stood there.... That is my explanation."
"Too clever! No, my friend, that is too clever. That beats everything."
"But why? Why?"
"Because everything fits together too neatly... it is too melodramatic."
"Ha!" Razumihin was exclaiming, but at that moment the door opened and a person walked in who was a stranger to everyone present.
